title: Democratic Socialists and American politics
text:
I have been following the recent rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and how they currently fit into the 2-party system and relationship to the Democratic party itself. I heard this interview with one of the co-chairs of DSA (Megan Romer is one, the other is Ashik Siddique) and also the recent flap with her on FOX news. I was deeply underwhelmed by her depth or response to the questions from David Remnick the host. 

The DSA will be the bogeyman that the GOP (and Trump) will use in the upcoming elections to tie some of the poorly articulated (and extreme views) of the DSA to the Democratic party. Importantly, the membership of the DSA is only 95,000 (out of about 72M each for the 2 main parties). Their strategy is to be provocative, insurgent, and to get attention. Democrats represent a "big tent" party, where there is a spectrum of diverse positions on economics (jobs, tax, capital vs. labor), national security (borders, police, foreign policy), and culture issues (gender, guns, religion). It is critical for the mainstream democrats to call out the extreme policy positions that are simply untenable. All politics are local and what is appropriate in NYC is different from Iowa. 

Hot button issues that make the headlines are easy to dispense with:

1. Healthcare: "Medicare for all" is an aspirational slogan, but we are very far from such a structure for a host of realities and a dysfunctional healthcare ecosystem;

2. Everyone needs security (i.e. we can't abolish police or prisons), and a country needs a border and enforcement (despite atrocious excesses of ICE); 

3. There is significant wealth inequality in our capitalistic economy, we already have many social programs that are beloved (SS), and there are many credible proposals to improve the current system (but Marx is not the solution, and there is no model country out there that the US should try to replicate); we can have a healthy debate about wealth tax, capital gains rate vs. ordinary income;

4. Middle East is a hot mess, Israel of course has a right to exist, 10/7 attack was barbaric which requires condemnation of Hamas, as is the slaughter of Gazans (however you label it); and a longer term 2-state solution is what is required but has been elusive for decades; this is a nice position articulated by Tom Friedman:
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/11/opinion/abdul-el-sayed-michigan-jews-israel-mamdani-aipac.html?smid=url-share

5. AI is deeply impactful and is upending all industries, and thoughtful regulations to foster equitable sharing of the benefits and costs will be needed, topic de jure of the decade;
6. Culture issues: live and let live!

I did not hear anything resembling common sense from Megan Romer!  If she is the face of the DSA, then I can see why many of the rising young candidates distancing themselves from the DSA platform.

To be sure, let’s not forget the vitriol and “what aboutism”, and patent falsehoods coming from the other side (Trump) and crickets from the GOP:  too many to list specifically!

Midterms is an opportunity for a referendum on the first 2 years of Trump 2.0, and a chance for change and reset.

Current key elections to monitor:

The House math

This is why I'd currently characterize the House as Democrats favored, but certainly not assured.

The GOP has far more seats exposed. The consensus analysis finds:

13 Republican-held toss-ups
vs.
2 Democratic-held toss-ups.

Democrats only need +3.

Moreover, the current national generic-ballot environment cited by the Almanac analysis is roughly a D+7 national environment. If that shift occurred uniformly, the analysis estimates Democrats would flip about 14 Republican-held competitive districts, comfortably enough to win the House.

So, the House is no longer simply "a toss-up." The structural battlefield currently tilts toward a Democratic takeover.

Senate: much tougher math for Democrats

Republicans currently control the Senate 53â47, meaning Democrats effectively need a four-seat net gain to take control.

The Senate battlefield is much smaller. The races I would put on your short list are:

Tier 1 — likely to determine control

North Carolina — open Republican seat. Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper gives Democrats perhaps their strongest pickup opportunity.

Maine — Republican Susan Collins remains one of Democrats' premier targets, although Collins has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to outperform Maine's Democratic lean.

Georgia — Democratic-held seat that Republicans need to contest seriously.

Michigan — Democratic-held/open-seat dynamics make this one of the critical Democratic defenses.

Those four states—especially NC, Maine, Georgia and Michigan—form the central Senate battlefield.

Then there are the states that could turn a good Democratic year into a Senate-changing wave:

Ohio — increasingly competitive.

Alaska — surprisingly competitive; recent handicapping has moved it toward toss-up territory.

Texas — still Republican-leaning, but important because Democrats almost certainly need to win at least one race beyond their easiest targets to reach 51.

The difficulty is obvious: Democrats can't merely win North Carolina and Maine. They have to protect their own vulnerable seats and find additional Republican pickups.
